definition: Tabling is a technique first developed for natural language processing, where it was called Earley parsing.
details: It consists of storing in a table (a.k.a. chart in the context of parsing) partial successful analyses that might come in handy for future reuse. Tabling consists of maintaining a table of goals that are called during execution, along with their answers, and then using the answers directly when the same goal is subsequently called. Tabling gives a guarantee of total correctness for any (pure) Prolog program without function symbols. Tabling can be extended in various directions. It can support recursive predicates through SLG resolution or linear tabling. In a multi-threaded Prolog system tabling results could be kept private to a thread or shared among all threads. And in incremental tabling, tabling might react to changes.

explainer.lead: Tabling stores the goals a logic program calls and the answers they produce, so a repeated call is answered from the table instead of recomputed. It matters because it removes much of the non-termination and repeated-work behaviour of naive evaluation.

tiers.eli5: Like writing down each homework question you have already solved, so when the same question comes up again you copy the answer instead of solving it twice.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use tabling to make recursive queries terminate and to avoid exponential re-derivation; the pitfall is the memory and table-space cost when many distinct goals are called.
tiers.paperLevel: Maintains a table of called goals with their answers; when the same goal is called again, the stored answers are used directly. Tabling guarantees total correctness for any pure Prolog program without function symbols.

explainer.example: A recursive reachability query calls the same subgoal for a node twice; the second call returns the tabulated answer immediately rather than recursing again.
